# Laurel Run Trailer Works, Inc. — company profile

**Fictional case, as of October 31, 2026.** Laurel Run, every person and every dealer, supplier, product and company figure in this case are invented for academic use. Hollow Glen is an invented Pennsylvania community, not a real street address. This is not a profile of any actual manufacturer. The operating accounts below are deliberately constructed assumptions, not observations, audited figures, or forecasts. Software names and the linked research sources are real.

Laurel Run is a family-owned, Pennsylvania-based builder of light open utility, enclosed cargo and equipment trailers. The company sells to approximately 80 independent dealers, not directly to retail customers; dealers set their own retail prices. As of the snapshot it employs exactly 50 people. One factory in fictional Hollow Glen houses cutting, welding, paint, final assembly, inspection, inventory and administration. Incoming freight is handled at the receiving bay; dealers arrange or accept delivery by appointment.

Elwood Bellamy, a fictional fabricator, founded the business in 1988 and retired in 2018. His children Mara, Owen and Tessa Bellamy work in the business: Mara is president and CEO, Owen is plant manager, and Tessa manages dealer sales. The Bellamy family owns the company. Elwood is not an employee and is not included in the headcount. The company added enclosed cargo trailers in the 2000s and the equipment family in the 2010s. These milestones are invented.

## TTM economics: November 1, 2025–October 31, 2026

Recognized revenue is wholesale dealer revenue for trailers shipped, including separately priced factory options, plus replacement parts sold to dealers. Sales are recognized at shipment, when the fictional standard sales terms transfer control to the dealer. Amounts collected as sales tax are excluded; the company does not separately bill freight in this illustrative year. Dealers' retail sales are not Laurel Run revenue. The shipped and completed quantities are both 1,500 because the fictional beginning and ending finished-trailer counts are the same.

| Revenue component | Units | Fictional net dealer amount | Revenue |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Trailfield 6×12 open utility, base | 600 | $4,800 per unit | $2,880,000 |
| Enclosure 7×14 enclosed cargo, base | 550 | $9,600 per unit | $5,280,000 |
| Workspan 82-inch × 18-foot equipment, base | 350 | $12,000 per unit | $4,200,000 |
| Factory options on those trailers | — | Aggregate; no assumption that every unit has the same options | $300,000 |
| Replacement parts sold to dealers | — | Aggregate | $90,000 |
| **Total** | **1,500 trailers** | | **$12,750,000** |

The option total is equivalent to $200 per shipped trailer on average, not a mandatory option charge. All three base amounts are the invented dealer net realized base prices for the year; this simplified scenario assumes no base-price discounts in this year. Total revenue per snapshot employee is **$255,000**. Total trailer base and option revenue is $12,660,000, or $8,440 per shipped trailer on average; parts revenue is separate.

|---|---:|---:|

| **Gross profit** | **$1,912,500** | **15.0%** |
| Office and selling wages and employer costs | ($900,000) | |
| Selling and marketing | ($160,000) | |

| **Total operating expenses** | **($1,530,000)** | **12.0%** |

Gross margin is gross profit divided by revenue; operating margin is operating income divided by revenue, before interest and income taxes. These are whole-dollar, deliberately chosen scenario inputs. Allocated production depreciation is in factory overhead; office depreciation is in operating expenses. Payroll costs are classified according to where the employee works, with mixed roles allocated. Owner-employees' compensation is included. The table does not purport to be a cash-flow statement.

**Research basis, not evidence of Laurel Run's actual results:** The [2022 Census SUSB size data](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/susb/tables/2022/us_state_naics_detailedsizes_2022.txt), summarized in `../research/02_economics.md`, imply about $255,216 receipts per employee for enterprises of 20–49 in the broader travel-trailer-and-camper category. That is a noisy 2022 aggregate ratio, not a 2026, 50-person, non-RV-company average. The 15% gross and 3% operating margins are selected assumptions informed by imperfect larger-company RV and commercial-trailer comparisons, not measured small-utility-trailer benchmarks; classification, cycle and cost allocation differ. The [BLS occupational data](https://www.bls.gov/oes/2023/may/naics4_336200.htm) support the plausibility of a production-heavy structure, not this exact roster. The `../research/` notes distinguish source findings and illustrative inferences.

document_chunks.heading: A straightforward open hauler

I own the inventory and purchasing records and review what we have and what is coming. The working stock list is an Excel sheet on the shared office drive. I want to know what is actually here, in the unit we use for that item, before I weigh it against an open order or what we are likely to need.

**Interviewer:** Where does your responsibility end and Cora's begin?

document_chunks.name: interviews/04_inventory_counting_interview.md
document_chunks.text:
**SME:** Cora does the weekly hand count and updates the stock sheet. I review the count, including any differences, and use the updated on-hand information when deciding order quantities. Cora reports to me, as does Jalen Sorrell, our Buyer. I report to Owen Bellamy, the Plant Manager. The count is not the same thing as receiving, although Cora also checks incoming goods against purchase orders.

**Interviewer:** What is the regular trigger, and how much of the inventory does it cover?

document_chunks.name: interviews/04_inventory_counting_interview.md
document_chunks.text:
**SME:** The routine is weekly. Cora counts six selected, frequently used SKU categories, not every item in the building. The estimate for counting and interpreting those selected lines is about an hour and a half in a working week, with the routine running over roughly 50 working weeks in the year. That's a workload estimate, not a time study for every count. It doesn't tell you the time for a full inventory.

**Interviewer:** Who chooses the six, and is it always the same selection?

**SME:** I'm not sure of the exact selection rule or whether the same six are counted every week. What I can point to is the October 30 sample: it shows six selected lines on that date. It doesn't provide all the other weekly rounds. I would not use that one sample to say we've physically verified the entire stock list.

document_chunks.name: interviews/04_inventory_counting_interview.md
document_chunks.text:
**Interviewer:** If I asked for a full inventory value at the snapshot, could this count give me that?

**SME:** No. I'm not sure what the total value of all inventory was. The sample is an on-hand example, not a complete ledger, valuation, or reconciliation to the general ledger. The selected materials catalog is not a complete bill of materials either. Those limits matter when someone is trying to make a larger claim from a small set of lines.

document_chunks.name: interviews/04_inventory_counting_interview.md
document_chunks.text:
**Interviewer:** Walk me through the count itself, from Cora arriving at the selected material to the point at which you review it.

**SME:** She hand-counts the selected stock and writes the physical counts on paper first. Each physical quantity is compared with the quantity on the Excel stock sheet before the count. The variance is physical count less that pre-count sheet quantity. Cora updates the Excel sheet with the physical count, and the paper count is kept with the inventory records. I review the count and any difference.

**Interviewer:** What do you need on that count record to make the comparison understandable later?

document_chunks.name: interviews/04_inventory_counting_interview.md
document_chunks.text:

If you only see the updated balance, you can't tell whether it agreed with the sheet before the count. The before and after are different facts, even when they happen to be the same number. The sample identifies Cora as counter and me as reviewer; it doesn't supply a complete history of all count activity.

**Interviewer:** You emphasized the unit. What can go wrong in the discussion if we leave it out?

**SME:** We could talk past each other. Axles are counted as each, rectangular steel tube in lengths, mounted wheels as assemblies, and floor screws in boxes. For SKU-0012 a box contains 250 screws. A difference of one box is not a difference of one loose screw. The item identification matters as well: two axle lines are not interchangeable just because both are axles.

document_chunks.name: interviews/04_inventory_counting_interview.md
document_chunks.text:
**Interviewer:** Is QuickBooks where the shop checks the physical quantity?

**Interviewer:** And an open purchase order wouldn't be counted among those physical pieces?

I compare the shipping records with the dealer invoice records for the period. If something doesn’t line up, I go back to the underlying shipping or invoice record and ask Mateo or Elena for the missing detail as appropriate. I don’t have to make up a particular discrepancy to explain that route. The point is that an unresolved item stays open for review.

**Interviewer:** And how does the management summary come out of that?

document_chunks.name: interviews/06_payroll_and_time_cards_interview.md
document_chunks.text:
**Interviewer:** Nia, could you start with your part of payroll and the point at which it becomes your work? I’m interested in the actual sequence, not just the name of the system.

**SME:** I’m the Office and Payroll Administrator, and I report to Lydia Fenner, our Controller. I collect the time information and prepare payroll. The period is 14 days, but I think about it as two separate Sunday-through-Saturday workweeks. We have 26 biweekly periods in a year. People record their time or exceptions, the hourly cards go to the appropriate approvers, and then the approved cards come to me. I prepare the weekly amounts, enter them, check them against the cards, review totals with Lydia and submit payroll.

**Interviewer:** What do people put on the card before it ever reaches you?

document_chunks.name: interviews/06_payroll_and_time_cards_interview.md
document_chunks.text:
**SME:** The hourly employees record start and end times, breaks and weekly totals on paper cards. There are 36 hourly employees in the snapshot. Thirty-two are shop employees, and that includes our two working supervisors; the other four are in office, receiving and shipping roles. For the 14 salaried employees, the routine uses paper exception notices rather than hourly cards.

**Interviewer:** What does an exception notice tell you compared with the card?

**SME:** It’s the paper notice used for a salaried employee’s exception. I’m not sure of the full set of circumstances or the detailed fields on that notice from these records. I wouldn’t turn the illustrative salaried hours in the sample into time-card entries or assume that a blank regular-hours field is an exception notice. They’re different records for different purposes.

document_chunks.name: interviews/06_payroll_and_time_cards_interview.md
document_chunks.text:
**Interviewer:** Are those categories the same thing as a legal overtime classification?

**SME:** No. “Hourly” and “salary” describe the pay basis in this roster; pay basis alone doesn’t establish someone’s legal overtime classification. The sample leaves the salaried regular and overtime fields blank, and that blank doesn’t answer the classification question either. If you ask me for a determination on an individual beyond the information here, I’m not sure; I wouldn’t make one from the shape of the spreadsheet.

**Interviewer:** And your own workload—does payroll occupy your whole job?

**SME:** No. The role matrix estimates my time at about 80 percent HR and payroll, 15 percent finance and accounting, and 5 percent facilities and administration. Those are approximate shares, not separate jobs. Payroll is an important part of the work, but it isn’t everything I do.

document_chunks.name: interviews/06_payroll_and_time_cards_interview.md
document_chunks.text:
**Interviewer:** Take me through the approval handoffs. Who has to see the cards before they reach you?

**SME:** Theo Lowry, the Fabrication Supervisor, signs for his direct reports, and Avery Carver, the Assembly Supervisor, signs for hers. They both work with their crews and have their own hourly cards, too. For the sample period, their manager, Plant Manager Owen Bellamy, is the planned approver of those two cards. I want to be precise there: that’s the planned routing for the sample, not evidence that he has already signed them.

**Interviewer:** What about the hourly people who aren’t on those crews?

document_chunks.name: interviews/06_payroll_and_time_cards_interview.md
document_chunks.text:
**SME:** Lydia is the relevant approver for Elena Corwin, the Accounting Clerk. Mara Bellamy, our President and CEO, is the approver for Holly Darnell, Reception and Admin Coordinator. Devon Kersey, Materials and Purchasing Manager, is the approver for Cora Whitlock in receiving and inventory and Mateo Renshaw in shipping. After the appropriate approval, the cards come to me.

**Interviewer:** So if I saw a supervisor’s name on a card, that would mean the supervisor is the employee, the approver, or both?

document_chunks.text:
**Interviewer:** Suppose you get a card and a time or signature is unclear. How do you handle it?

**SME:** I check with the employee and the relevant approver. It might be a start or end time, a break, a weekly total or a signature that’s missing or unclear. The corrected card goes back for the appropriate signoff. I can’t just fill in an hour because it looks likely, and a card that hasn’t arrived isn’t zero hours. If it cannot be resolved, I bring it promptly to Lydia for direction.

**Interviewer:** Is that a description of a specific problem in the October sample?

document_chunks.name: interviews/06_payroll_and_time_cards_interview.md
document_chunks.text:
**SME:** No, I’m describing the procedure if that happens. I’m not sure how many cards needed correction in that period; the summary doesn’t say. Until the question is settled, I don’t have a clean approved figure to treat as established.

**Interviewer:** If you’re away, who takes over submission?

**SME:** I’m not sure. The procedure says to bring an unresolved case, or my absence, promptly to Lydia for direction. It doesn’t name a backup payroll submitter or an alternate card approver. I wouldn’t substitute Lydia’s direction for an invented assignment of those roles.

document_chunks.name: interviews/06_payroll_and_time_cards_interview.md

document_chunks.name: interviews/06_payroll_and_time_cards_interview.md

document_chunks.text:

document_chunks.name: interviews/06_payroll_and_time_cards_interview.md
document_chunks.text:

processes.name: Dealer Quoting & Sales Coordination
processes.description: Priya Ellwood handles dealer requests via Outlook or calls, checks IDs against an Excel list, and populates a quote template. Tessa Bellamy approves quotes, manages the pricing/formula workbook, and handles approximately 100 exceptional pricing questions annually. Quotes are offers until written acceptance.

processes.name: Order Intake & Production Scheduling
processes.description: Upon written dealer acceptance, Priya creates an order in Excel and a paper build packet. Jonah Sutter assigns unique WO identifiers, sets target dates (estimates, not guarantees), sequences work weekly in Excel/whiteboard, and hands packets to the floor. Supervisors report progress or exceptions back to Jonah for schedule updates.
pain_points: Target dates treated as promises by dealers

processes.name: Purchasing, Receiving & Inventory Management
processes.description: Devon Kersey oversees purchasing; Jalen Sorrell creates POs. Cora Whitlock hand-counts 6 frequent SKUs weekly, updates an Excel stock sheet, and records receipts against POs. Exceptions go to Devon. QuickBooks is used for bills only; Excel and paper serve as the working shop-floor counts.
pain_points: Discrepancy between accounting system (QuickBooks) and working inventory (Excel/paper)
Manual cycle counting of only 6 SKUs
Shortage handling causes worker idle time

processes.name: Shipping, Invoicing & Month-End Close
processes.description: Mateo Renshaw schedules shipments and sends confirmations. Elena Corwin issues dealer invoices in QuickBooks at shipment (net 30). Lydia Fenner oversees monthly close: bank/AP/AR reconciliation, shipping vs invoice comparison, management summary export/re-keying to Excel, and checklist signoff.
pain_points: Close timeline often extends beyond 5-day target
No named backup for Controller signoff

processes.name: Warranty Claims & Returns Processing
processes.description: Priya receives dealer warranty messages, forwards details/photos to Iris Calder. Iris opens claims (CLM-YYYY-NNNN), verifies components, approves dealer repairs before work starts, and closes claims upon completion evidence. No blanket coverage rule exists; each claim is reviewed individually.
pain_points: No backup repair approver if Iris is unavailable
Manual tracking via Excel index/email threads

processes.name: Payroll & Time Card Administration
processes.description: Nia Hadley collects paper time cards/exception notices, resolves omissions, enters biweekly hours into RUN Powered by ADP, reviews totals with Controller Lydia Fenner, and submits payroll. 36 hourly staff use cards; 14 salaried use exception notices. Supervisors approve direct reports' cards.
pain_points: Unclear legal overtime classification based on pay basis alone
No named backup payroll submitter or approver

scored_opportunities.name: Quote Template Auto-Populator & Credit Checker
scored_opportunities.what_the_agent_does: Monitors Priya's Outlook inbox for dealer requests, extracts vehicle specs and dealer ID, cross-references the ID against the Excel approval list, auto-fills the quote template, and flags pricing exceptions for Tessa's review.
scored_opportunities.gap: Manual Excel template management and ambiguous credit status handling require Priya to manually copy-paste data and guess credit eligibility.
scored_opportunities.rating_reason: High value by saving Priya hours on template population and exception routing; moderate effort requires Outlook/Excel API connectors; low risk as it only assists manual review and approval.

scored_opportunities.name: WO Identifier & Schedule Sync Agent
scored_opportunities.what_the_agent_does: Converts written dealer acceptance into a unique WO ID, auto-generates the paper build packet, and updates Jonah's Excel/whiteboard schedule with target dates while flagging potential sequencing conflicts.
scored_opportunities.gap: Manual re-keying between quote/order/register and target dates treated as promises without system validation.

scored_opportunities.name: Cycle Count & PO Reconciliation Agent
scored_opportunities.what_the_agent_does: Monitors QuickBooks bills and Jalen's POs, triggers automated cycle counts for the 6 frequent SKUs when stock drops below threshold, and flags shortages to Devon automatically.
scored_opportunities.gap: Discrepancy between QuickBooks and Excel/paper counts, plus manual cycle counting of only 6 SKUs causes idle time.
scored_opportunities.rating_reason: High business value by preventing production stoppages and closing the accounting/working inventory gap; higher effort requires multi-system sync; moderate risk as false shortages impact floor efficiency.

scored_opportunities.name: Management Summary Auto-Reconciler
scored_opportunities.what_the_agent_does: Extracts shipping confirmations and QuickBooks invoices, compares them automatically, generates the monthly management summary, and flags discrepancies for Lydia before close.
scored_opportunities.gap: Manual re-keying of management summaries and close timeline extending beyond 5-day target.
scored_opportunities.rating_reason: Directly attacks the 5-day close target and manual re-keying pain point; moderate effort for data extraction setup; low risk since it serves as a pre-close validation tool rather than auto-approving.

scored_opportunities.name: Warranty Coverage Rule Engine & Tracker
scored_opportunities.what_the_agent_does: Maintains a centralized knowledge base of warranty terms, auto-routes Priya's dealer messages to Iris with pre-verified component details, and tracks claim status (CLM-YYYY-NNNN) to prevent manual Excel/email tracking.
scored_opportunities.gap: Ambiguous warranty terms/coverage rules and manual tracking via Excel index/email threads.
scored_opportunities.rating_reason: Solves ambiguous coverage and manual tracking issues; moderate effort due to knowledge base creation; higher risk because incorrect warranty rulings directly impact margins and dealer relations.

scored_opportunities.name: Time Card Digitizer & Overtime Classifier
scored_opportunities.what_the_agent_does: Scans paper time cards and exception notices, extracts hours, validates against legal overtime rules based on pay basis (not just hours), and pre-populates RUN Powered by ADP for Nia's review.
scored_opportunities.gap: Manual paper-to-system data entry and unclear legal overtime classification based on pay basis alone.
scored_opportunities.rating_reason: High value by removing 36 manual entries and clarifying overtime compliance; high effort due to OCR setup and complex rule engine; moderate risk as payroll errors carry legal consequences but are caught by Nia/Lydia.

scored_opportunities.name: Dealer & Component Master Data Cleanup

roadmaps.rationale: This sequence deliberately avoids high-complexity integrations by tackling the lowest-risk data consolidation first, which prevents downstream errors in sales and financial reporting. The quoting automation follows as a natural extension of the cleaned master data, while postponing the inventory reconciliation ensures you do not prematurely expose fragile purchasing workflows to automated triggers. This careful progression matches your low risk tolerance by building confidence through predictable, low-impact implementations before touching critical supply chain operations.
roadmaps.pilot_reason: The Master Data Cleanup is piloted first because it operates entirely within existing spreadsheets and requires no external system connections, minimizing implementation failure risk.
roadmaps.assumption: Your team must consistently maintain the source Excel files and pricing formulas, as any manual overrides outside the cleanup process will immediately corrupt the automated workflows.
